articles.title: Araqchi: Iran discussed ideas with Qatari mediators, Hormuz conditions must be met
articles.description: The remarks suggest the Qatari mediation channel is live, but they also show Iran tying any Hormuz reopening to conditions it has not spelled out, which keeps a supply risk premium in oil. Crude has been trading in both directions on each new diplomatic headline, and firm language from Tehran could limit downside if traders had been leaning on the earlier reports of possible sanctions relief. The next catalyst is the US reply, which will be relayed through Qatar, so any sign of movement on sequencing, or a breakdown, is likely to drive the next leg in Brent and WTI. --- Earlier: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, calls Axios report a hoax --- Iran is keeping the diplomatic door open through Qatar while insisting the Supreme Leader's conditions must be met before the Strait of Hormuz reopens. Summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran discussed ideas with Qatari mediators that are to be put to the US, according to IRNA. He said the US response will be conveyed to Tehran through the Qatari mediators. Araqchi said the conditions stressed by Iran's Supreme Leader must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen. He added that if the US wants an agreement or a peaceful solution, Iran has already presented one. The comments follow Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz proposal on Saturday and a disputed Axios report on possible US sanctions relief. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said late Monday that Tehran had discussed ideas with Qatari mediators that are to be put to the United States, according to Iran's IRNA news agency. He said the US response will be conveyed back to Tehran through the same Qatari channel. Araqchi also said the conditions stressed by Iran's Supreme Leader must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen. He added that if Washington wants an agreement or a peaceful solution, Iran has already presented one. The reports did not detail the ideas discussed with the mediators or spell out the conditions he referred to. The comments follow a weekend in which US President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait. US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Trump turned it down because it required the immediate lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen assets. Qatari mediators had been expected to hold separate talks with the Iranian and US sides on Monday or Tuesday, focused on an amended version of a seven-day proposal that Iran presented last week, according to an official cited by Reuters. Axios reported earlier on Monday, citing US officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds in return for concrete progress on the nuclear issue. One US official described the indirect talks as positive and constructive, while saying gaps remain on timing and on who takes which steps first. Trump later denied on Truth Social that he had offered Iran anything and called the Axios report a hoax. Oil traded on the diplomatic headlines throughout Monday. Brent settled around $105 a barrel after an early jump of more than $4 faded, and the earlier reports of possible sanctions relief had coincided with softer crude. Middle East exports have recovered in recent weeks, though flows through the strait remain below pre-conflict levels. Attention now turns to the US response that will be passed to Tehran via Qatar, and to whether the mediators can narrow the gaps on sequencing before Iran's conditions for reopening the strait are tested. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle's 'gatekeeper' alarms as 'problematic' deals come to light: 'Sketchy'
articles.description: One of President Donald Trump's foreign ambassadors has been hanging out with someone during her time in Greece, which has raised red flags among some of the administration's critics. The Wall Street Journal reported that Kimberly Guilfoyle , Trump's ambassador to Greece, has been frequently seen with Christos Marafatsos, a 39-year-old lobbyist who, some officials said, has often cosplayed as Guilfoyle's chief of staff during meetings with government officials. "These days, the Maryland-raised Marafatsos is frequently seen at Guilfoyle’s side, acting as her unofficial gatekeeper and joining her for meetings at her ambassadorial residence and with government officials in countries around the region — a highly unusual move for a private citizen," the report reads in part. Robin Brooks, a former foreign service official with more than two decades of experience, described Marafatsos' behavior to the WSJ as "absolutely problematic" because it calls into question whether the meeting is advancing American interests or advancing some sort of private interest.” Several political analysts sounded the alarm over Guilfoyle and Marafatsos' relationship on Sunday. "Sketchy," Molly Jong-Fast, a political commentator and MS NOW host, posted on X. "They [are] inventing weird new kinds of corruption," journalist Matthew Yglesias posted on X. "Unprecedented corruption," Brendan Nyman, a political scientist at Dartmouth, posted on X.

articles.title: Trump says he's 'very seriously' looking at a diesel export ban
articles.description: (Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he is still looking “very seriously” at implementing a US ban on diesel exports to combat high prices, even as others in his administration continue to focus on other possible steps. Most Read from Bloomberg Kroger Sets New Dress Code Rules for Its Grocery-Store Workers Ellison Pledges $9.2 Billion More in Oracle Shares for Loans Canadian Oil No Longer Takes Long Road to Asia as Freight Surges McDonald’s Selloff Hits 30% as Big Mac Inflation Spurs Pushback Florida’s Private Railroad Brightline Files for Bankruptcy “That can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we’re looking at it very seriously — we may do it,” Trump told a Fox News reporter Sunday while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament final near Chicago. Several farm-state lawmakers have urged Trump to limit US diesel exports during the peak of the fall harvest season, as global fuel markets reel from the disruption to flows in the critical Strait of Hormuz and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. The US has emerged as the supplier of last resort to the world, with diesel exports surging to a weekly record near 2 million barrels a day last month. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have been analyzing the ramifications of a potential short-term ban on US diesel exports over the last week, underscoring the seriousness of the administration’s consideration of the idea. Oil CEOs and industry groups have pushed instead for suspending the federal diesel excise tax, saying it would ease prices without the drawbacks of an export ban. But that’s been met with internal debate about how to waive the tax — especially with the House of Representatives in a pre-election recess. Diesel powers farm equipment, freight trains, trucks and delivery vans. US retail prices hit a record last week and are averaging about $6.50 a gallon, adding to voter anxiety over living costs before November’s midterm elections. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week that the administration is working with refiners on voluntary export curbs as an alternative to a government-imposed ban. Some companies are already adding contractual protections in the event a pause on diesel shipments overseas prevents deliveries to foreign buyers, people with knowledge of the situation told Bloomberg News Friday. In the event of a ban, US diesel prices would be widely expected to plummet, at least in the short run. A halt would leave America’s allies, including Brazil and the UK, urgently needing to secure fuel.
